headline: D.C. medical cannabis sales hit record $10.8M in October 2026
dek: D.C.'s medical cannabis sales reached $99.8 million through October, near all of 2025, and self-certified visitors bought nearly a third of dispensary sales.
key_points: D.C.'s medical cannabis market sold a record $10.79 million in October 2026, up 20.4% from October 2025, according to ABCA data reported by The Marijuana Herald.
Sales for January to October reached $99.85 million, about $1.06 million short of all of 2025's $100.9 million.
Self-certified temporary patients from outside D.C. spent $2.1 million at dispensaries in October, about 31% of dispensary sales by our arithmetic.
That self-certification route is the same feature the DEA cited when it said no D.C. operator can qualify for federal registration.
body: The District of Columbia's medical cannabis market had its best month on record in October. Combined sales reached $10,785,487, up 5.3% from September and 20.4% from October 2025, according to monthly figures from the District's Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration (ABCA), as reported by The Marijuana Herald. That beat the previous 2026 high of about $10.61 million set in July.

Sales for the first ten months of 2026 reached $99,845,126. By our arithmetic, the District needs about $1.06 million more to pass all of 2025's $100.9 million, a gap October's pace would close within the first week of November. The growth comes even as the District's operators face a federal problem: the DEA has said none of them can qualify for registration under Schedule III.

Licensed dispensaries took in $6,748,855 in October, up 16.8% from a year earlier. Manufacturers reported $3,258,936, up 32.3%, and cultivation centers $777,696, the Herald reported from the ABCA data. The District had 68 licensed retailers in October, one more than in September.

The buyer mix is the most telling number. District residents accounted for $4,237,980 of dispensary purchases. Self-certified temporary patients from outside the District spent $2,099,301, and patients using reciprocity from other medical programmes spent $411,575. By our arithmetic, residents made up about 63% of dispensary sales, self-certified visitors about 31% and reciprocity patients about 6%.

Temporary patient registrations rose to 13,303 in October from 12,823 in September. Virginia supplied the most, 4,718, followed by Maryland at 1,957, North Carolina at 896, Texas at 634 and Florida at 569. Virginia alone was about 35% of temporary registrations by our arithmetic.
> Nearly a third of D.C.'s dispensary sales rely on the self-certification route the DEA says disqualifies the whole market.

Registered District resident patients reached 153,828 in October, up 4,629 in a month, and the number of unique patients served by dispensaries rose from 40,736 to 42,298, according to the Herald. Flower remained the largest category at $3,338,702 for 729 pounds sold. By our arithmetic, that is about $10.10 per gram. Vape cartridges brought in $1,246,163, edibles $826,941 and raw pre-rolls $749,722. Beverage sales doubled in unit terms to 2,000 drinks for $24,628, still a small slice of the total.

Only a minority of registered patients shop in a given month. The 42,298 unique patients served in October equal about 27% of registered residents, and dispensary sales work out to roughly $160 per unique patient for the month, by our arithmetic. Visitors and reciprocity patients are counted in that sales figure, so spending per resident is lower.
October was the sixth month this year with combined sales above $10 million, and monthly revenue has stayed above $9 million since March, the Herald said.

The record comes as the District's businesses sit outside the federal system that Schedule III created. As we reported on 8 November, the DEA moved to deny a D.C. medical dispensary and said it cannot register any operator under the District's rules, because patients there can self-certify rather than obtain a written certification. The agency rested that on the Single Convention's prescription requirement. As we reported on 12 November, the District was also among the jurisdictions where the DEA sent orders to show cause to medical businesses.

The October data show how much of the market that ruling touches. The self-certified visitor channel was worth about $2.1 million in a single month at dispensaries. If the District tightened self-certification to satisfy the DEA, that revenue would be at risk; if it does not, its operators stay outside federal registration and the tax relief that comes with it. That trade-off is our assessment.

The District's biggest out-of-town customer base may also shrink on its own. Virginia lawmakers are preparing for adult-use retail sales to begin in 2027, and Virginians are the largest group of temporary patients in the District. Once Virginia residents can buy legally at home, some of the $2.1 million monthly visitor spend could move across the Potomac.

Watch ABCA's November figures to confirm when 2026 passes 2025's total, any change to the District's self-certification rules in response to the DEA, the outcome of the DEA's show-cause proceedings against District businesses, and the DEA's 29 November supply-chain deadline for applicants elsewhere.
